article.title: Remembering Peter D. Thomas (1973–2026)
article.author: Panagiotis Sotiris
article.content: It is with immense sadness and grief that we share the news of the death of our comrade, friend and long-standing member of the Historical Materialism Editorial Board Peter D. Thomas. Peter passed away due to a heart-attack on 11 October 2026, just after he had turned 53. With an academic background in philosophy and literature from his studies in Australia, having obtained a BA and an MA from the University of Queensland, he came to Europe to pursue his doctoral research in 2000. His PhD at the University of Amsterdam was supervised by Marcel van der Linden and Michael R. Krätke, and was awarded in 2008 despite efforts by right-wing members of the University to derail it. What started as a thesis that attempted an immanent critique of Perry Anderson’s and Louis Althusser’s respective readings of Gramsci – a thesis written under not always easy funding conditions – ended up as perhaps the most original contribution to Gramsci studies in the twenty-first century. Combining the insights, philological and exegetical, of the Italian research on Gramsci that followed the publication of the critical edition of the Notebooks by Valentino Gerratana, with a non-dogmatic and non-sectarian reading of revolutionary Marxism, Peter produced a highly innovative reading of Gramsci. He understood Gramsci as a militant thinker of open questions of revolutionary practice, politically and intellectually, by both stressing the notion of the integral state and through an insistence on the radical novelty of Gramsci’s philosophy of praxis. In contrast to traditional readings of Gramsci as a theorist of hegemony as consent, and beyond denunciations of Gramsci’s historicism or reformism, Peter managed to bring to the fore the full experimental richness of Gramsci’s carceral research project, demonstrating how it confronted questions of revolutionary strategy. The Gramscian Moment: Philosophy, Hegemony and Marxism stressed Peter’s ability to combine philological fidelity to Gramsci’s text with a broader engagement with the history of political theory while maintaining a constant focus on the open strategic questions associated with the traditions of revolutionary Marxism. Peter’s writings on Gramsci, on Marx and on Marxism would only make more evident the creative and insightful character of his work, in particular his insistence that hegemony referred to an experimental and pedagogical subaltern political practice aiming at emancipation as transformation. His entries in Das Historisch-kritische Wörterbuch des Marxismus and the Dizionario gramsciano, his articles on the question of organisation, on the modern prince, his highly original return to the notion of the passive revolution, his writings on the subaltern, subalternity and translatability, and his 2023 book on Radical Politics: On the Causes of Contemporary Emancipation , were superb attempts to use his reading of Gramsci as a way to confront contemporary radical politics. But Peter was much more than simply a Gramsci specialist, he was one of the most original political theorists of his generation, combining deep knowledge of the history of political theories with an acute awareness of how they could be read in light of contemporary challenges. The scope of his work was broad and included not only Marxism but also the broader traditions of political philosophy and theory. Combining scholarly brilliance with a respect and understanding for political militancy and its exigencies, he understood how the new anticapitalist radicalism of the beginning of the twenty-first century had to seriously engage with theory. The originality and creativity of his thinking are evident in his writing on Althusser, on the falling rate of profit, on Lenin and dual power, in the book he co-authored with Juha Koivisto on communication and media research, but also in the volumes he co-edited on Althusser, plural temporalities, and Marx’s Grundrisse as laboratory. At the time of his untimely death, he was working on the final stages of a project funded by the Leverhulme Trust exploring the different contexts, conditions and consequences of the translation of hegemony in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Italian and German philosophical, social and political thought. Peter had a distinctive style, evident not only in his writing but also in his conference presentations. It was complex, dialectical, and nuanced, managing to combine semantic density with exemplary clarity, philologically grounded, yet able to make novel connections. During his research Peter spent time in Italy, in Germany, in Finland and in the Netherlands, including the time spent at the Jan van Eyck Academy in Maastricht, which led to an important co-edited volume on Althusser. At each stage, he seriously engaged with theoretical and political traditions but also with the local Marxist scene, building bonds that lasted. When he arrived at Brunel University in 2010, where he eventually becameProfessor and Head of Department, Peter left behind the precarious conditions that had marked a significant period of his early research, only to face the pressures of an increasingly commercialised UK academic system. He was a marvellous teacher, supervisor, and mentor, gifted with the generosity generosity that so many, in the wake of his passing, readily acknowledge There are theorists who we remember primarily for their lectures and articles, but Peter is also remembered for the discussion after the lecture, after the presentation, the insights he would share, the email exchanges, the encouragement and the constructive criticism. With his wry sense of humour and genuine attentiveness to what his interlocutors had to say, he made every conversation a truly formative experience. Peter was of course more than his research. He joined the Editorial Board of Historical Materialism during the preparation of his PhD thesis in the early 2000s and played a very important role both in the functioning of the journal as well as the London conferences, becoming one of the most recognisable faces of what was to become the most important international network of scholarly debate on Marxism. He also played a very central role in the Historical Materialism Book Series , soliciting manuscripts, helping authors improve their works, and turning them into one of the most important Marxist publishing project in the anglophone world. For us on the Historical Materialism Editorial Board, he was both our comrade and friend, not only part of our monthly meetings and endless emails and threads on journal and conference issues, but also part of the conference team and of discussions, stories and laughs at the traditional drinks at the Marlborough Arms pub after the end of each London Conference. We are still struggling to comprehend why the brightest light among us has been snuffed out so early. With Sara Farris and their two daughters, Mira and Nadia, aged 12 and 7, they created a beautiful family, and Peter was a wonderful loving and caring partner and father. Death came unexpectedly, at a moment when he was more creative than ever, working on new projects, putting a premature and unjust end to a trajectory that had yet so much to offer. At the same time, his work so far has already had a significant impact and will continue to be studied and debated in the years to come. For us the loss is great and the grief is deep. We have lost our comrade, and we already miss our friend. In the weeks and months to come we will honour his memory by returning to his work and inviting comrades to share their thoughts. Above all, we will continue to work in the manner we are sure he wanted us to work: unapologetically Marxist yet beyond any dogmatism and stubbornly insisting that good theory and comradely scholarly debate remain indispensable aspects of any attempt towards emancipatory politics today. But right now, our thoughts and hearts are with Sara, Mira and Nadia, and Peter’s broader family.
